justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift assumption from what I'd take as a baseline price near 420 for the S&P 500 ETF (SPY) or a similar broad index instrument. For the one-day horizon, the estimate of 421.5 reflects very little expected movement, essentially assuming markets open and close near current levels with only a slight positive bias drawn from the long-run historical tendency for equity markets to drift higher over time. The one-week estimate of 423 extends that drift slightly further, and the one-month estimate of 426 continues that trajectory, incorporating roughly a 1–1.5% annualized upward tilt compounded over the respective horizons. These estimates are not driven by any specific catalyst but rather by the baseline assumption that absent major shocks, equity markets tend to grind modestly higher.

The confidence interval widths reflect well-established patterns in realized volatility at different time horizons. For the one-day interval (412–431), I'm using something close to a typical daily volatility of around 1–1.2% annualized to roughly 20% annualized, which translates to about a 1.2–1.5 point daily standard deviation scaled to a 90% interval. The one-week interval widens by roughly the square root of five, and the one-month interval widens further still by the square root of roughly 21 trading days. This square-root-of-time scaling is the standard assumption under random walk dynamics, though in practice volatility clusters and can spike dramatically, meaning the true tails are fatter than a normal distribution would imply.

Several specific risks could push outcomes well outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected Federal Reserve policy surprise, a significant deterioration in economic data signaling recession, an escalation in geopolitical conflict, or a credit event in a systemically important institution could easily produce a 5–10% drawdown within even a single week, pushing prices well below the lower bounds I've stated. On the upside, a surprisingly strong earnings season, a ceasefire in an active conflict, or an unexpected dovish pivot from central banks could generate a sharp rally beyond the upper bounds. My intervals essentially represent normal market conditions; they are not stress-tested against tail scenarios, which remain meaningful probabilities over a one-month horizon.

It is also worth acknowledging that my forecast was made without real-time data, so I may be anchoring on a stale baseline price. If the actual current price differs meaningfully from my assumed starting level, all three point estimates and intervals should be shifted accordingly.
